questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.
questions.a: Propan-1-amine. A wrong answer like "propylamine" reveals the student is using common naming instead of IUPAC; "propanamine" (missing locant) reveals they forgot the mandatory locant for the amino group on a chain longer than two carbons.

questions.q: Explain why the compound CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ is named N-methylethanamine and not methylethylamine.
questions.a: In IUPAC, secondary amines are named as N-substituted alkanamines: the larger alkyl group (ethyl) becomes the parent "ethanamine", the smaller (methyl) is an N-substituent with locant N. "Methylethylamine" is a common name; IUPAC requires the 'N-' prefix to show substitution on nitrogen, not carbon. A student writing "methylethylamine" confuses common and IUPAC systems.

Propan-2-amine. Steps: 1) Longest chain = 3 carbons → propane. 2) –NH₂ on carbon-2 → locant 2. 3) Replace -e with -amine → propan-2-amine. Wrong answer "isopropylamine" uses common name; "2-aminopropane" uses incorrect prefix style (aminopropane is not IUPAC for primary amines).

questions.q: Compare the IUPAC names of CH₃CH₂NH₂ and C₆H₅NH₂. Why does the aromatic amine retain the 'e' in "benzenamine" while the aliphatic amine drops the 'e' in "ethanamine"?
questions.a: Aliphatic: alkane (ethane) → drop 'e' + amine = ethanamine. Aromatic: arene (benzene) → replace 'e' with 'amine' = benzenamine (NCERT rule). Actually both drop 'e'; the difference is the parent hydrocarbon name. A student saying "aniline" for C₆H₅NH₂ uses the accepted trivial name but misses the systematic "benzenamine". The rule is consistent: parent hydride name minus 'e' plus 'amine'.

questions.q: A student writes the name of (CH₃CH₂)₃N as "triethylamine". Is this correct IUPAC? If not, give the correct name and explain the error.
questions.a: Incorrect. Correct IUPAC: N,N-diethylethanamine. The student used the common name. IUPAC for tertiary amines: choose one ethyl as parent (ethanamine), the other two as N,N-diethyl substituents. Error: using multiplicative prefix 'tri-' on the alkyl group without 'N,' locants and without identifying the parent alkanamine.

questions.q: Design a systematic method to name any aliphatic amine (primary, secondary, tertiary) given its structure. Write the steps as a flowchart.
questions.a: Flowchart: 1) Count carbons in each alkyl group attached to N. 2) Identify the largest alkyl group → parent alkanamine (name = alkane minus 'e' + 'amine'). 3) Number parent chain to give –NH₂ (or >NH) lowest locant. 4) Remaining alkyl groups on N become N-substituents with prefixes di/tri and locant N. 5) Assemble: N-substituents (alphabetical) + parent name. A poor answer misses step 3 (locant on chain) or step 4 (N-locant).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: IUPAC nomenclature of amines systematically names amines by identifying the parent alkane chain (for aliphatic amines) or arene (for aromatic amines), indicating the position of the amino group(s) with locants, and using prefixes (di-, tri-) for multiple amino groups; for secondary and tertiary amines, the alkyl/aryl groups attached to nitrogen are designated with the locant 'N' (e.g., N-______).
Fill in the blank: Observe a medicine strip of "Cetirizine" (an antihistamine) — its chemical name contains "diamine" and "chloro" ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly write the IUPAC name for any given aliphatic or aromatic amine structure (primary, secondary, tertiary, or polyfunctional) and can draw the structure from a given IUPAC name, applying the correct locants, prefixes, and 'N'-substituent notation without errors.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Observe a medicine strip of "Cetirizine" (an ______) — its chemical name contains "diamine" and "chloro" substituents.
